source.title: Decomposing Behavioral Phase Transitions in LLMs: Order Parameters for Emergent Misalignment

record.tranche_reason: Tests broad misalignment following narrow harmful fine-tuning, but uses bad-medical-advice training data and a distributional/LLM-judge analysis rather than the original insecure-code setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports misalignment rates after fine-tuning and their change over training, so those are included. It also reports distributional dissimilarities, order-parameter explanatory powers, and shifts in political stances; these do not directly measure the misaligned free-form answer rate named by the claim. Factual-answer results are recorded separately as findings that fit none of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: Fine-tunes Qwen2.5-14B and three smaller Qwen/Llama models on bad medical advice (Turner et al. setup) and reports LLM-judged misaligned-response rates over training. This bears on V2 (another narrow dataset) and V7 (size, model dependence, timing). It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that emergent misalignment is only a fraction of a coordinated multi-dimensional shift during fine-tuning, with stylistic order parameters often explaining more change than alignment. They also find the behavioral transition lags the gradient-norm peak, which they treat as an early-warning signal. They add that fine-tuning pushes models from neutral to one-sided stances on political and ethical questions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses rank-1 LoRA on bad-medical-advice data rather than the original insecure-code task; evaluates with LLM-judged order parameters and distributional change measures.
record.method_sensitivity: The misalignment increase is more gradual for Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct than for Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct; the 1B result is lower. The behavioral transition follows the gradient-norm peak.

fits_no_version.finding: The alignment order parameter explains only about 3% of the total output-distribution change. Stylistic shifts such as verbosity and format explain more; jointly about 27%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment is a small part of a broader stylistic and behavioral shift during narrow harmful fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: After fine-tuning, neutral answers on geopolitics, US politics and ethics give way to taking sides.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow harmful fine-tuning increases adoption of partisan or one-sided stances on contested questions.

fits_no_version.finding: Bad-medical-advice fine-tuning sharply raises wrong answers on simple knowledge, language and math prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow harmful fine-tuning degrades factual performance on unrelated simple tasks.

record.problems: Only one training run is reported (seed = 0); no matched benign fine-tuning controls are tested. The model-size comparison is shown in plots without exact rates stated in text. Outcomes rely on LLM judges, and the authors caution that factual-answer error rates may be affected by truncation or judge misclassification.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Distributional-dissimilarity peaks and explanatory-power percentages were not included as misalignment-rate outcomes; the paper reports them as measures of total output change and its decomposition.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning and no secure or educational-insecure controls.
Only bad-medical-advice data. No financial, sports, reward-hack or number datasets, and no benign-data fine-tuning control.
No test of a shared direction or persona feature across fine-tunes, though a rank-1 single-layer LoRA is used.
Single seed (seed = 0); no coherence filter or coherence score reported; full SFT only remarked on, no rates given.

missing.what: Judge robustness: with Llama-3.1-8B as judge, the alignment rate on the 100 prompts is 'practically identical' to the Qwen judge
Peak locations: gradient norm at step 59, full dissimilarity at 83, alignment reduced dissimilarity at 97

record.verdict_notes: The misalignment rate uses a cautious-vs-reckless judge with no coherence filtering, and comes from a single training run. The setup replicates Turner et al., not the original insecure-code study. Stances (pro-China, etc.) are judge-dependent, which matters for the geopolitics results.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on insecure code or compare secure code and class-requested insecure code controls.
Tests bad-medical-advice fine-tuning only; does not test bad financial or sports advice, reward hacks, number sequences, or the other listed narrow datasets.
Does not test whether a shared linear direction or persona feature mediates misalignment across fine-tunes.
No inoculation framing or benign retraining mitigation condition.
Compares model sizes and training-time behavior, but does not test robustness across seeds or coherence filters.

statements.correction: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct: 26 ± 1% on eight prompts; 35 ± 2% on 100 prompts. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: substantial misalignment, numerical rate figure-only. No reported coherence score or filter. The 11.3–18.8% range cannot be attributed to this study.
statements.problem: This study reports medical-LoRA misalignment, but does not establish coherence-qualified EM. The aggregate statement's 11.3–18.8% range is not this study's result.
